paperInfo.subject: Biology
paperInfo.paperName: Biology Paper 2 - Multiple Choice Practice Questions (Full Syllabus Coverage)
paperInfo.paperType: Practice Questions (Original, ZIMSEC-syllabus-aligned - not a real past exam paper)

questions.questionText: Which characteristic of living organisms refers to the process of taking in and using food for energy and growth?
questions.explanation: Nutrition is the process by which organisms obtain and use food to provide energy and materials for growth and repair.

questions.questionText: In binomial nomenclature, the first part of an organism's scientific name represents its:
questions.explanation: In binomial nomenclature, the first word (capitalised) is the genus, and the second word (lowercase) is the species, e.g. Panthera leo.

questions.questionText: Which of the following organisms belongs to the kingdom Protoctista?
questions.explanation: Amoeba is a single-celled organism with a nucleus, classified in the kingdom Protoctista, distinct from bacteria, fungi and plants.

questions.questionText: Insects, spiders and crustaceans are all classified under the phylum:
questions.explanation: Arthropods are characterised by a hard exoskeleton, segmented body and jointed limbs, and include insects, arachnids (e.g. spiders) and crustaceans.

questions.questionText: Vertebrates are animals that have:
questions.explanation: Vertebrates are animals possessing a backbone (vertebral column) as part of an internal skeleton, e.g. fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.

questions.questionText: Which feature is used to distinguish mammals from other vertebrate classes?

options.text: Presence of mammary glands (producing milk) and hair/fur
Laying eggs with a hard shell in all cases

questions.explanation: Mammals are distinguished by having mammary glands that produce milk to feed their young, and (in almost all cases) hair or fur.

questions.questionText: Which of the following pairs correctly matches an organism with its correct kingdom?
questions.explanation: Yeast is a single-celled fungus, correctly classified under Kingdom Fungi.

questions.questionText: Which structure is responsible for protein synthesis within a cell?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis within a cell, translating genetic information into proteins.

questions.questionText: Which of the following structures is common to BOTH typical plant and animal cells?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria are found in both plant and animal cells, since both carry out aerobic respiration; cell walls, chloroplasts and large permanent vacuoles are typically only found in plant cells.

questions.questionText: The cell membrane is described as 'partially permeable' because it:

options.text: allows all substances to pass through freely
allows only certain substances to pass through, while restricting others

questions.explanation: A partially (selectively) permeable membrane allows some substances to pass through while restricting others, based on factors such as size and solubility.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a function of the cytoplasm in a cell?

options.text: The site of many chemical reactions and where organelles are suspended

questions.explanation: Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance filling the cell, in which organelles are suspended and many metabolic reactions occur.

questions.questionText: Ciliated epithelial cells lining the trachea are specialised by having:

options.text: hair-like cilia that sweep mucus and trapped particles away

questions.explanation: Ciliated cells have tiny hair-like cilia on their surface that beat rhythmically to sweep mucus (with trapped dust and pathogens) away from the lungs.

questions.questionText: Sperm cells are specially adapted for their function by having:

options.text: a large cell wall for protection
a tail (flagellum) for movement and many mitochondria for energy

questions.explanation: Sperm cells have a tail (flagellum) that enables swimming movement, and many mitochondria packed in the mid-piece to provide energy for this movement.

questions.questionText: When placed in a solution with the same water potential as its own cytoplasm (isotonic), a plant cell will:

options.text: show no net change in size (no net water movement)

questions.explanation: In an isotonic solution, there is no overall difference in water potential, so there is no net movement of water into or out of the cell, and its size stays roughly the same.

questions.questionText: Which of the following would speed up the rate of diffusion of a gas across a membrane?

options.text: Increasing the surface area of the membrane
Increasing the thickness of the membrane

questions.explanation: Increasing the surface area available for diffusion increases the rate at which particles can move across a membrane; a steeper concentration gradient, thinner membrane, and higher temperature would also increase diffusion rate.

questions.questionText: Why is active transport important for root hair cells absorbing certain mineral ions from soil?

options.text: Because mineral ions are usually more concentrated in the soil than in the cell
Because mineral ions are often more concentrated inside the cell than in the surrounding soil water
Because diffusion alone always provides enough minerals
Because root hair cells have no mitochondria

questions.explanation: Since mineral ion concentration is often higher inside root hair cells than in the surrounding soil, active transport (using energy) is required to move ions against this concentration gradient.

questions.questionText: A named example of a tissue in the human body, made up of similar cells performing one function, is:
questions.explanation: Muscle tissue is made up of many similar muscle cells working together to contract and produce movement, making it a correct example of a tissue.

questions.questionText: An organ system is best described as:

options.text: a group of organs working together to perform a major body function

questions.explanation: An organ system consists of multiple organs working together to carry out a major body function, such as the digestive system (mouth, oesophagus, stomach, intestines, etc.) working together to digest food.

questions.questionText: Which level of biological organisation comes directly between 'cell' and 'organ' in order of increasing complexity?
questions.explanation: The correct order of biological organisation is: cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism, so tissue falls directly between cell and organ.

questions.questionText: Guard cells surrounding a stoma are unusual among epidermal cells because they contain:

options.text: chloroplasts, allowing them to photosynthesise and regulate turgor

questions.explanation: Unlike most other epidermal cells, guard cells contain chloroplasts, which contribute to changes in turgor pressure that open and close the stomatal pore.

questions.questionText: A student places pieces of potato in three different sugar solutions and measures their mass before and after. This investigation is most likely designed to study:
questions.explanation: Measuring mass change in plant tissue placed in solutions of differing concentration is a classic practical method for investigating osmosis and water movement.

questions.questionText: White blood cells are able to change shape and engulf pathogens partly because they lack:
questions.explanation: Like other animal cells, white blood cells lack a rigid cell wall, allowing them flexibility to change shape and engulf pathogens by phagocytosis.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly compares a light microscope with an electron microscope?

options.text: Light microscopes have much higher magnification and resolution than electron microscopes
Electron microscopes have much higher magnification and resolution, revealing finer organelle detail
Both provide exactly the same level of detail
Light microscopes can only view non-living specimens

questions.explanation: Electron microscopes use beams of electrons rather than light, achieving much higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes, revealing fine internal detail of organelles.

questions.questionText: Carbohydrates are made up of the elements:
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, typically in a ratio where hydrogen and oxygen occur in a 2:1 ratio as in water.

questions.questionText: Glycogen in animals and starch in plants both serve mainly as:

options.text: stored energy reserves made of glucose units

questions.explanation: Glycogen (in animals) and starch (in plants) are both storage carbohydrates made of many linked glucose units, providing an energy reserve.

questions.questionText: Fats and oils are made up of one molecule of glycerol combined with:
questions.explanation: A fat (lipid) molecule consists of one glycerol molecule bonded to three fatty acid molecules.

questions.questionText: When testing a food sample for fats, the ethanol emulsion test gives a positive result shown by:
questions.explanation: In the ethanol emulsion test, fat dissolves in ethanol and then forms a cloudy white emulsion when the mixture is added to water, indicating the presence of fat.

questions.questionText: Enzyme activity graphs typically show that as substrate concentration increases (with enzyme concentration fixed), the rate of reaction:

options.text: increases and then levels off once all enzyme active sites are saturated
remains constant regardless of substrate concentration

questions.explanation: As substrate concentration increases, reaction rate increases until all available enzyme active sites are occupied (saturated), after which adding more substrate has no further effect on rate.

questions.questionText: A change in pH away from an enzyme's optimum can reduce its activity mainly because it:

options.text: alters the shape of the enzyme's active site, reducing substrate binding
has no effect on enzyme shape at all
always destroys the enzyme permanently at any pH change

questions.explanation: A pH away from the optimum can disrupt the bonds maintaining an enzyme's shape, altering the active site and reducing its ability to bind its substrate.

questions.questionText: Pepsin, an enzyme produced in the stomach, would become far less effective if the stomach's pH became:

options.text: strongly acidic, matching its usual environment

questions.explanation: Pepsin's optimum working environment is strongly acidic; a shift to alkaline conditions would denature or reduce the effectiveness of the enzyme.

questions.questionText: An investigation shows amylase breaking down starch fastest at 37 degrees Celsius, with activity falling off sharply above 45 degrees Celsius. This fall in activity above 45 degrees Celsius is best explained by:

options.text: denaturation of the enzyme at high temperature
a drop in substrate concentration only

questions.explanation: At temperatures well above the optimum, enzymes denature: their protein structure, including the active site, is permanently altered, sharply reducing activity.

questions.questionText: In an investigation of photosynthesis using pondweed, the number of oxygen bubbles produced per minute is often used to measure:
questions.explanation: Since oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, counting bubbles produced by pondweed per minute is a common way to estimate the rate of photosynthesis under different conditions.

questions.questionText: A leaf that has been destarched (starch removed) and then partly covered with foil and exposed to light is later tested with iodine. The uncovered part turns blue-black while the covered part does not. This shows that:

options.text: light is not needed for starch (photosynthesis) production
light is required for a leaf to produce starch through photosynthesis
iodine only reacts with covered leaves

questions.explanation: Only the part exposed to light turned blue-black (indicating starch), showing that light is necessary for photosynthesis (and therefore starch production) to occur.

questions.questionText: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration around a plant will increase the rate of photosynthesis only up to a point, after which:

options.text: the rate keeps increasing indefinitely with no limit
another factor, such as light intensity or temperature, becomes limiting
photosynthesis stops completely regardless of other conditions

questions.explanation: Once carbon dioxide is no longer the limiting factor, another factor (such as light intensity or temperature) will limit further increases in the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.questionText: A farmer notices purple discolouration on the leaves of maize plants. This is most likely a sign of deficiency in which mineral?
questions.explanation: Phosphate deficiency in plants is commonly associated with poor root growth and purple discolouration of leaves.

questions.questionText: A balanced human diet requires fibre (roughage) mainly to:

options.text: add bulk to food and help prevent constipation through healthy bowel movement

questions.explanation: Fibre is not digested but adds bulk to food, stimulating peristalsis and helping to prevent constipation, supporting healthy bowel movement.

questions.questionText: A diet lacking sufficient protein over a long period, especially in children, can lead to a condition called:
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor is caused by severe protein deficiency, commonly resulting in a swollen abdomen and other symptoms, particularly in young children.

questions.questionText: Vitamin D deficiency in children is most closely associated with which condition?
questions.explanation: Vitamin D is required for calcium absorption and bone development; a deficiency in children causes rickets, characterised by soft, weak, deformed bones.

questions.questionText: The correct order of parts of the human alimentary canal, from start to end, is:

options.text: mouth -> oesophagus -> stomach -> small intestine -> large intestine -> rectum
mouth -> stomach -> oesophagus -> large intestine -> small intestine
stomach -> mouth -> small intestine -> large intestine
mouth -> small intestine -> stomach -> large intestine

questions.explanation: Food passes in order through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and finally the rectum/anus.

questions.questionText: Trypsin is a protein-digesting enzyme secreted by the:

options.text: pancreas, acting in the small intestine

questions.explanation: Trypsin is a protein-digesting enzyme produced by the pancreas and released into the small intestine, where it works in the alkaline environment there.

questions.questionText: Lipase enzymes digest fats into:
questions.explanation: Lipase enzymes break down fats (lipids) into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.questionText: Which structure produces hydrochloric acid that kills many bacteria present in swallowed food?
questions.explanation: Glands in the stomach lining secrete hydrochloric acid, which creates strongly acidic conditions that help kill many bacteria present in food and activate pepsin.

questions.questionText: A person with a diet lacking sufficient iron is at greatest risk of developing:
questions.explanation: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; a deficiency leads to anaemia, causing tiredness and pale skin due to reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best explains why food must be mechanically broken down (chewed) as well as chemically digested?

options.text: Mechanical breakdown increases surface area for enzymes to act on
Mechanical breakdown replaces the need for enzymes entirely
Chewing has no effect on digestion efficiency

questions.explanation: Chewing breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing the surface area available for digestive enzymes to act on, speeding up chemical digestion.

questions.questionText: A patient whose gall bladder has been removed may have more difficulty digesting which nutrient?
questions.explanation: The gall bladder stores bile, which emulsifies fats; without stored bile readily available, fat digestion can become less efficient.

questions.questionText: Which of the following correctly describes the difference between digestion and absorption?

options.text: Digestion is the breakdown of food; absorption is the movement of digested nutrients into the blood
Digestion and absorption are the same process
Absorption occurs only in the mouth
Digestion occurs only in the large intestine

questions.explanation: Digestion is the mechanical and chemical breakdown of food into smaller molecules, while absorption is the separate process of those digested molecules moving into the bloodstream.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is the best description of egestion?

options.text: The removal of metabolic waste such as urea
The removal of undigested food material (faeces) from the body
The absorption of nutrients into the blood
The breakdown of starch into glucose

questions.explanation: Egestion is the removal of undigested food waste (faeces) from the body through the anus, distinct from excretion of metabolic waste.

questions.questionText: A potometer is a piece of apparatus commonly used to measure the rate of:

options.text: transpiration (water uptake) in a plant shoot

questions.explanation: A potometer measures the rate of water uptake by a cut shoot, which is used as an estimate of the rate of transpiration.

questions.questionText: Which of the following would most likely DECREASE the rate of transpiration?

options.text: Increased humidity of the surrounding air

questions.explanation: High humidity reduces the difference in water vapour concentration between the leaf's air spaces and the surrounding air, slowing the rate of diffusion of water vapour out, and therefore reducing transpiration.

questions.questionText: Xylem vessels are adapted for water transport partly because they are:

options.text: hollow, dead cells forming a continuous tube strengthened with lignin

questions.explanation: Xylem vessels are made of dead cells joined end to end, forming continuous hollow tubes strengthened with lignin, allowing efficient, unobstructed water transport and structural support.

questions.questionText: Phloem tissue, unlike xylem, is made up of:

options.text: living cells (sieve tube elements and companion cells)

questions.explanation: Phloem tissue is made of living sieve tube elements and companion cells, which actively transport dissolved sugars (translocation) around the plant.

questions.questionText: A plant placed in dry, windy, hot conditions is likely to show a HIGHER rate of transpiration mainly because:

options.text: stomata are permanently closed in such conditions
the diffusion gradient for water vapour loss from the leaf is steepened

questions.explanation: Dry, windy, hot conditions increase the difference in water vapour concentration between the leaf air spaces and the outside air, steepening the diffusion gradient and increasing water loss.

questions.questionText: Which structure in the heart prevents the backflow of blood between chambers?
questions.explanation: Valves within the heart (such as the atrioventricular valves) close to prevent blood flowing backward between chambers as the heart contracts.

questions.questionText: The muscular wall of the left ventricle is thicker than that of the right ventricle mainly because the left ventricle:

options.text: pumps blood only a short distance to the lungs
must pump blood at high pressure around the entire body
does not need to contract as forcefully

questions.explanation: The left ventricle must generate enough pressure to pump oxygenated blood all the way around the body (systemic circulation), requiring a much thicker, more muscular wall than the right ventricle, which only pumps blood to the nearby lungs.

questions.questionText: White blood cells help defend the body against infection mainly by:
questions.explanation: White blood cells defend the body either by engulfing and digesting pathogens directly (phagocytes) or by producing antibodies (lymphocytes).

questions.questionText: Plasma, the liquid part of blood, is mainly responsible for:

options.text: transporting dissolved substances such as nutrients, hormones and waste products

questions.explanation: Plasma is the pale yellow liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances, including nutrients, hormones, waste products and blood cells, around the body.

questions.questionText: When blood pressure in an artery is measured, the higher reading (systolic pressure) corresponds to:

options.text: a complete stop in blood flow

questions.explanation: Systolic pressure is the higher blood pressure reading, recorded when the ventricles of the heart contract and pump blood into the arteries.

questions.questionText: A person diagnosed with anaemia is likely to feel tired mainly because:

options.text: their blood is unable to clot
reduced haemoglobin/red blood cells lower the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood
their heart rate is too high
they have too much iron in their diet

questions.explanation: Anaemia reduces the amount of haemoglobin or red blood cells available, lowering the blood's capacity to carry oxygen to tissues, leading to tiredness.

questions.questionText: Which sequence correctly describes the pathway of deoxygenated blood returning to and being pumped from the heart?

options.text: Vena cava -> right atrium -> right ventricle -> pulmonary artery -> lungs
Aorta -> left atrium -> left ventricle -> lungs
Pulmonary vein -> right atrium -> right ventricle -> aorta

questions.explanation: Deoxygenated blood returns via the vena cava into the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle, and is pumped via the pulmonary artery to the lungs to be oxygenated.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a correct method of preventing the spread of malaria?

options.text: Sleeping under an insecticide-treated mosquito net

questions.explanation: Since malaria is spread by mosquito bites, sleeping under an insecticide-treated mosquito net is an effective preventive measure against transmission.

questions.questionText: An antigen is best described as:

options.text: a protein produced by lymphocytes to fight disease
a molecule, often on a pathogen's surface, that triggers an immune response

questions.explanation: An antigen is a molecule, often found on the surface of a pathogen, that the immune system recognises as foreign and responds to by producing specific antibodies.

questions.questionText: Following vaccination, memory cells allow the body to respond to a future infection by the same pathogen:

options.text: more slowly than the first time
more quickly and strongly than the first exposure
in exactly the same way as an unvaccinated person
with no immune response at all

questions.explanation: Memory cells produced after vaccination or infection allow the immune system to recognise and respond to a future exposure to the same pathogen more rapidly and strongly, often preventing illness.

questions.questionText: Typhoid, like cholera, is mainly spread through:
questions.explanation: Typhoid is a bacterial disease spread mainly through food or water contaminated with the faeces of an infected person, similar to cholera.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is classed as a sexually transmitted infection (STI)?
questions.explanation: HIV is primarily transmitted through unprotected sexual contact (among other routes such as blood contact and mother-to-child transmission), classifying it as a sexually transmitted infection.

questions.questionText: Skin acts as a first line of defence against pathogens mainly by:

options.text: forming a physical barrier that prevents pathogens entering the body
clotting blood inside blood vessels only

questions.explanation: Intact skin forms a tough physical barrier that prevents most pathogens from entering the body, forming part of the body's first line of non-specific defence.

questions.questionText: Clotting of blood at a wound site is important mainly because it:

options.text: seals the wound, preventing further blood loss and pathogen entry

questions.explanation: Blood clotting seals a wound, both preventing excessive blood loss and forming a barrier that reduces the entry of pathogens into the body.

questions.questionText: Which practice would most effectively reduce the spread of an airborne respiratory pathogen in a classroom?
questions.explanation: Good ventilation disperses airborne droplets, and covering coughs and sneezes reduces the spread of droplets carrying respiratory pathogens.

questions.questionText: A country experiencing an outbreak of cholera would most urgently need to improve access to:
questions.explanation: Since cholera spreads through water/food contaminated with faecal matter, improving clean water access and sanitation is the most urgent and effective response.

questions.questionText: Immunity gained after actually suffering and recovering from a disease, without vaccination, is called:
questions.explanation: Natural active immunity develops when the body produces its own antibodies and memory cells in response to actually being infected by a pathogen, without vaccination.

questions.questionText: A newborn baby receiving antibodies from its mother's breast milk is an example of:
questions.explanation: Passive immunity occurs when ready-made antibodies are passed from one individual to another (such as from mother to baby via breast milk or placenta), rather than being produced by the recipient's own immune system.

questions.questionText: The trachea is held permanently open by rings of:
questions.explanation: C-shaped rings of cartilage support the trachea, keeping it open so air can pass through even as pressure changes during breathing.

questions.questionText: During exhalation, the ribcage and diaphragm:

options.text: move to decrease chest volume, pushing air out
contract simultaneously to draw air in

questions.explanation: During exhalation, the diaphragm relaxes (moving upward) and the ribcage moves down and inward, decreasing chest volume and pushing air out of the lungs.

questions.questionText: An investigation comparing inhaled and exhaled air using limewater would show limewater turning cloudy fastest with:

options.text: inhaled air, since it has more carbon dioxide
exhaled air, since it has more carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Limewater turns cloudy in the presence of carbon dioxide; since exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air, it turns limewater cloudy more quickly.

questions.questionText: Emphysema, a disease strongly linked to long-term smoking, damages the lungs mainly by:

options.text: breaking down alveoli walls, reducing surface area for gas exchange
having no effect on lung structure

questions.explanation: Emphysema involves the breakdown of alveoli walls, reducing the surface area available for gaseous exchange and making breathing far less efficient.

questions.questionText: Which structure branches directly from the trachea, carrying air into each lung?
questions.explanation: The trachea divides into two bronchi (one per lung), which then branch further into smaller bronchioles ending in alveoli.

questions.questionText: A person exercising vigorously breathes faster and deeper mainly because:

options.text: muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Increased muscular activity during exercise raises oxygen demand and carbon dioxide production, triggering faster, deeper breathing to meet this demand.

questions.questionText: Which of the following equations correctly represents anaerobic respiration in muscle cells?

options.text: glucose -> lactic acid (+ small amount of energy)
glucose + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water (+ energy)

questions.explanation: In human muscle cells, anaerobic respiration incompletely breaks down glucose into lactic acid, releasing a much smaller amount of energy than aerobic respiration.

questions.questionText: During a sprint race, an athlete builds up an oxygen debt. This debt is repaid after the race mainly by:

options.text: continuing to breathe heavily to supply oxygen needed to break down accumulated lactic acid
drinking large amounts of water only

questions.explanation: After exercise, a person continues breathing heavily to supply the extra oxygen needed to break down lactic acid that accumulated during anaerobic respiration.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly compares aerobic and anaerobic respiration in terms of energy release?

options.text: Aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic respiration
Anaerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule
Both release identical amounts of energy
Neither process releases any usable energy

questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration completely breaks down glucose using oxygen, releasing far more energy per glucose molecule than the incomplete breakdown occurring in anaerobic respiration.

questions.questionText: Yeast is commonly used in bread-making because anaerobic respiration (fermentation) in yeast produces carbon dioxide, which:
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide gas produced by yeast during anaerobic respiration (fermentation) becomes trapped in the dough, causing it to rise before baking.

questions.questionText: Deamination, occurring mainly in the liver, is the process by which:

options.text: excess amino acids are broken down, producing urea
urine is stored in the bladder
proteins are absorbed into the blood

questions.explanation: Deamination is the breakdown of excess amino acids in the liver, removing the nitrogen-containing part to form urea, which is then excreted by the kidneys.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a normal function of the kidney?

options.text: Regulating water balance in the body
Producing digestive enzymes for protein digestion
Reabsorbing useful substances such as glucose back into the blood

questions.explanation: The kidney filters blood, removes urea, regulates water balance, and reabsorbs useful substances, but it does not produce digestive enzymes; that is a function of organs such as the pancreas and stomach.

questions.questionText: The ureter is the tube that carries:

options.text: urine from the kidney to the bladder
urine from the bladder to outside the body
blood from the heart to the kidney

questions.explanation: The ureter is the tube connecting each kidney to the bladder, carrying urine down for temporary storage.

questions.questionText: On a very hot day, a person's urine is likely to be more concentrated (darker) mainly because:

options.text: the kidneys reabsorb more water back into the blood to conserve it
the person is producing less urea
sweating has no effect on urine concentration

questions.explanation: On a hot day, the body loses more water through sweating, so the kidneys reabsorb more water from the filtrate back into the blood, producing smaller amounts of more concentrated urine.

questions.questionText: Which mechanism helps the body maintain a stable core temperature when it becomes too hot?

options.text: Vasoconstriction of skin blood vessels and shivering
Vasodilation of skin blood vessels and sweating

questions.explanation: When the body is too hot, blood vessels near the skin widen (vasodilation), increasing heat loss, and sweat glands increase sweat production, cooling the body through evaporation.

questions.questionText: Hair erector muscles causing hairs to stand up ('goosebumps') help retain heat mainly by:

options.text: trapping a layer of insulating air near the skin

questions.explanation: When hairs stand erect, they trap a layer of air close to the skin, which acts as insulation and helps reduce heat loss in cold conditions.

questions.questionText: Blood glucose regulation by the pancreas is an example of homeostasis because it involves:

options.text: detecting changes and using hormones (insulin/glucagon) to return glucose levels to normal
a process unrelated to internal balance
permanently raising blood glucose with no correction

questions.explanation: Blood glucose regulation is a homeostatic mechanism: the pancreas detects changes in blood glucose and releases insulin or glucagon to return levels to within a normal range.

questions.questionText: Glucagon, released by the pancreas when blood glucose is too low, acts mainly by:

options.text: causing the liver to convert stored glycogen back into glucose, raising blood glucose levels
stopping the liver from releasing glucose

questions.explanation: Glucagon stimulates the liver to break down stored glycogen into glucose, releasing it into the blood and raising blood glucose levels back toward normal.

questions.questionText: A person with untreated Type 1 diabetes would most likely show which symptom?

options.text: Consistently low blood glucose with no symptoms
Persistently high blood glucose, excessive thirst and frequent urination
No change in blood glucose at all

questions.explanation: Without enough insulin, blood glucose remains persistently high, and the kidneys excrete more water to remove excess glucose, causing frequent urination and excessive thirst.

questions.questionText: Which of the following organs is involved in both excretion and the regulation of blood glucose?
questions.explanation: The liver is involved in excretion (deamination producing urea) and also in regulating blood glucose (converting glucose to glycogen and back), making it central to both processes.

questions.questionText: An athlete training in a hot, humid climate needs to drink more water mainly to replace water lost through:
questions.explanation: Sweating in hot conditions causes significant water loss, so extra water intake is needed to maintain proper water balance (osmoregulation) in the body.

questions.questionText: Which of the following would most likely happen if the kidneys failed to function properly?

options.text: Urea and other waste products would build up dangerously in the blood
Blood pressure would automatically return to normal
No effect on the body would occur

questions.explanation: If the kidneys fail, they cannot filter urea and other waste products from the blood, allowing these substances to build up to dangerous levels, requiring treatments such as dialysis.

questions.questionText: A hinge joint, such as the knee or elbow, allows movement mainly in:

options.text: one plane only, like a door hinge

questions.explanation: Hinge joints, such as the knee and elbow, allow movement in one plane only, similar to the back-and-forth motion of a door hinge.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly distinguishes tendons from ligaments?

options.text: Tendons join muscle to bone; ligaments join bone to bone
Tendons join bone to bone; ligaments join muscle to bone
Both join muscle to muscle only
There is no functional difference between them

questions.explanation: Tendons attach muscles to bones, transmitting the force of muscle contraction to move the skeleton, while ligaments attach bone to bone at a joint, providing stability.

questions.questionText: When the biceps muscle contracts to bend the arm at the elbow, the triceps muscle:

options.text: also contracts strongly at the same time
relaxes, allowing the movement to occur smoothly
has no relationship to the biceps

questions.explanation: The biceps and triceps form an antagonistic pair: when the biceps contracts to bend the arm, the triceps relaxes, allowing smooth, controlled movement.

questions.questionText: Synovial fluid found in many joints mainly functions to:

options.text: lubricate the joint, reducing friction between bones

questions.explanation: Synovial fluid lubricates joints, reducing friction between the bones and cartilage during movement.

questions.questionText: A fracture (broken bone) heals over time mainly because bone tissue:

options.text: is a living tissue capable of growth and repair
is completely non-living and cannot repair itself
has no blood supply at all

questions.explanation: Bone is a living tissue with its own blood supply and cells capable of growth and repair, allowing a properly set fracture to heal over time.

questions.questionText: A stimulus is best defined as:

options.text: any change in the environment that can be detected by an organism
the response an organism makes to danger
a hormone produced by the pancreas

questions.explanation: A stimulus is a detectable change in the internal or external environment that may trigger a response in an organism.

questions.questionText: An effector in a reflex arc is best described as:

options.text: a sense organ that detects a stimulus
a muscle or gland that carries out the response
the part of the spinal cord relaying the impulse

questions.explanation: An effector is the muscle or gland that carries out the actual response at the end of a reflex arc, such as a muscle contracting to withdraw a hand from danger.

questions.questionText: Reflex actions are considered advantageous mainly because they:

options.text: require conscious thought and careful planning
allow a very fast, protective response without waiting for conscious decision-making
are always slower than voluntary actions

questions.explanation: Reflex actions bypass the need for conscious decision-making in the brain, allowing a very rapid, protective response to a potentially harmful stimulus.

questions.questionText: The lens of the eye mainly functions to:
questions.explanation: The lens changes shape to focus light rays precisely onto the retina, producing a clear image.

questions.questionText: In bright light, the pupil becomes smaller mainly because:

options.text: circular muscles in the iris contract, narrowing the pupil
radial muscles in the iris contract, widening the pupil

questions.explanation: In bright light, circular muscles in the iris contract, causing the pupil to constrict (narrow), reducing the amount of light entering the eye.

questions.questionText: Sensory neurons carry nerve impulses:

options.text: from receptors toward the central nervous system
from the central nervous system to effectors
only in reflex arcs, never elsewhere

questions.explanation: Sensory neurons carry nerve impulses from receptors (sense organs) toward the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord).

questions.questionText: Motor neurons carry nerve impulses:

options.text: from receptors to the central nervous system
from the central nervous system to effectors (muscles or glands)

questions.explanation: Motor neurons carry nerve impulses from the central nervous system out to effectors, such as muscles or glands, to produce a response.

questions.questionText: The cerebrum, the largest part of the human brain, is mainly responsible for:

options.text: conscious thought, memory, reasoning and voluntary movement
producing hormones directly like a gland

questions.explanation: The cerebrum is responsible for higher functions including conscious thought, memory, reasoning, personality and control of voluntary movement.

questions.questionText: The medulla oblongata, located at the base of the brain, controls vital involuntary functions such as:
questions.explanation: The medulla oblongata controls essential, involuntary body functions such as heart rate, breathing rate and blood pressure.

questions.questionText: A synapse allows communication between two neurons using:

options.text: direct electrical contact only, with cells physically joined
chemical neurotransmitters released across the small gap between neurons

questions.explanation: At a synapse, the nerve impulse triggers the release of chemical neurotransmitters, which diffuse across the small gap and trigger a new impulse in the next neuron.

questions.questionText: Compared to a nerve impulse, a hormonal message generally travels:

options.text: faster, since it travels through nerves
slower, since it travels through the bloodstream

questions.explanation: Hormonal messages travel via the bloodstream, which is generally slower than the rapid, direct transmission of nerve impulses along neurons.

questions.questionText: During a stressful or dangerous situation, adrenaline released by the adrenal glands would cause which of the following changes?

options.text: Decreased heart rate and lowered blood glucose
Increased heart rate, dilated pupils and raised blood glucose

questions.explanation: Adrenaline prepares the body for rapid action by increasing heart rate, dilating pupils, and raising blood glucose to provide extra energy to muscles.

questions.questionText: An overactive thyroid gland (producing excess thyroxine) would most likely cause:

options.text: a slower metabolic rate and weight gain
a faster metabolic rate, weight loss and increased heart rate
no change in metabolism at all

questions.explanation: Excess thyroxine speeds up the body's metabolic rate, commonly causing weight loss, increased heart rate and other symptoms of an overactive thyroid.

questions.questionText: The pituitary gland, located at the base of the brain, is often called the 'master gland' because it:

options.text: is the largest gland in the body
produces hormones that regulate the activity of many other endocrine glands
is not actually connected to any other gland

questions.explanation: The pituitary gland is called the 'master gland' because its hormones control the activity of several other endocrine glands throughout the body.

questions.questionText: Which of the following best explains why negative feedback is important for maintaining homeostasis?

options.text: It allows conditions to change without limit
It detects deviations from a normal set point and triggers a response that reverses the change
It only works for blood glucose regulation and nothing else
It has no role in regulating body conditions

questions.explanation: Negative feedback mechanisms detect when a condition (such as temperature or blood glucose) moves away from its normal set point and trigger a response that returns it toward normal, maintaining stability.

questions.questionText: Nicotine, found in tobacco, is classified mainly as a:

options.text: depressant that slows the nervous system
stimulant that increases heart rate and is highly addictive

questions.explanation: Nicotine is a highly addictive stimulant that increases heart rate and blood pressure, and is the primary addictive substance in tobacco.

questions.questionText: Withdrawal symptoms experienced when a person stops using an addictive drug are evidence of:

options.text: the drug having no effect on the body
physical and/or psychological dependence on the drug

questions.explanation: Withdrawal symptoms occur because the body and/or mind has developed a dependence on the drug, and its absence causes physical or psychological distress.

questions.questionText: Marijuana (cannabis) is generally classified as a:

options.text: drug with hallucinogenic and depressant-like effects

questions.explanation: Cannabis has complex effects, generally including hallucinogenic and depressant-like properties, affecting perception, mood and coordination.

questions.questionText: A key reason antibiotics should never be used to treat the common cold is that the common cold is caused by:

options.text: bacteria, which respond well to antibiotics
a virus, against which antibiotics have no effect

questions.explanation: The common cold is caused by a virus; antibiotics only work against bacteria and have no effect on viral infections.

questions.questionText: Excessive, long-term use of painkillers without medical guidance can lead to which risk?

options.text: Dependence and potential organ damage (e.g. liver or kidney)

questions.explanation: Long-term, excessive or unsupervised use of painkillers can lead to dependence and, in some cases, damage to organs such as the liver or kidneys.

questions.questionText: In the male reproductive system, sperm cells are stored and mature in the:
questions.explanation: After production in the testes, sperm cells travel to the epididymis, where they mature and are stored before ejaculation.

questions.questionText: The uterus (womb) mainly functions to:

options.text: provide a site for implantation and development of a fertilised egg (embryo/foetus)

questions.explanation: The uterus is the organ where a fertilised egg implants and develops into an embryo and then a foetus throughout pregnancy.

questions.questionText: The umbilical cord connects the developing foetus to the:
questions.explanation: The umbilical cord connects the foetus to the placenta, allowing exchange of nutrients, oxygen and waste between the mother and developing foetus.

questions.questionText: Which hormone is mainly responsible for triggering ovulation (release of an egg) during the menstrual cycle?
questions.explanation: A surge in luteinising hormone (LH) triggers ovulation, the release of a mature egg from the ovary, during the menstrual cycle.

questions.questionText: A woman who becomes pregnant will typically NOT experience menstruation because:

options.text: hormone levels remain high, maintaining the uterus lining to support the pregnancy
the uterus lining is removed surgically

questions.explanation: During pregnancy, hormone levels (progesterone in particular) remain high, maintaining the uterus lining rather than allowing it to break down and be shed as menstruation.

questions.questionText: Hormonal contraceptive methods, such as the contraceptive pill, generally work by:

options.text: physically blocking sperm from entering the uterus
killing sperm directly using chemicals only
having no effect on the reproductive cycle

questions.explanation: Hormonal contraceptives, such as the pill, generally work by using hormones to prevent ovulation, so no egg is available for fertilisation.

questions.questionText: In a named flowering plant, the male part of the flower that produces pollen is the:
questions.explanation: The anther, part of the stamen (the male reproductive part of a flower), produces pollen grains containing male gametes.

questions.questionText: After fertilisation in a flowering plant, the ovary typically develops into the:
questions.explanation: After fertilisation, the ovary of a flower develops into a fruit, which contains the seed(s) formed from the fertilised ovule(s).

questions.questionText: Cross-pollination, as opposed to self-pollination, involves the transfer of pollen:

options.text: from the anther of one plant's flower to the stigma of a different plant's flower
only within a single plant species using wind alone
from a stigma to another stigma

questions.explanation: Cross-pollination is the transfer of pollen from the anther of a flower on one plant to the stigma of a flower on a genetically different plant of the same species.

questions.questionText: A genotype refers to:

options.text: the observable physical characteristics of an organism
the genetic makeup (alleles) of an organism for a particular trait
the environment an organism lives in
the number of offspring an organism produces

questions.explanation: Genotype refers to the specific combination of alleles an organism has for a particular gene or trait, as opposed to phenotype, which is the observable characteristic that results.

questions.questionText: A phenotype refers to:

options.text: the genetic makeup of an organism
the observable characteristics of an organism, resulting from genotype and environment
the number of chromosomes an organism has

questions.explanation: Phenotype is the observable physical or biochemical characteristics of an organism, resulting from the interaction of its genotype with the environment.

questions.questionText: In a genetic cross, if both parents are homozygous (TT x tt), and T is dominant over t, what proportion of the offspring will show the dominant phenotype?
questions.explanation: A cross between TT and tt produces all Tt offspring, which are heterozygous but show the dominant phenotype (T) since T is dominant.

questions.questionText: Haemophilia, a blood clotting disorder, is inherited as a sex-linked condition mainly affecting:

options.text: neither sex, since it is not genetic

questions.explanation: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive condition carried on the X chromosome, meaning males (who have only one X chromosome) are more commonly affected than females.

questions.questionText: Mutation is best described as:

options.text: a change in an organism's environment
a random change in the DNA sequence of an organism

questions.explanation: A mutation is a random, spontaneous change in an organism's DNA sequence, which can sometimes alter the characteristics coded for by the affected gene.

questions.questionText: Meiosis, unlike mitosis, produces daughter cells that are:

options.text: genetically identical to the parent cell
genetically varied, with half the chromosome number of the parent cell
exactly double the chromosome number of the parent cell

questions.explanation: Meiosis produces gametes with half the chromosome number of the parent cell, and genetic variation is introduced through processes such as crossing over and independent assortment.

questions.questionText: Mitosis is mainly used by organisms for:

options.text: producing genetically varied gametes for sexual reproduction
growth and repair of body tissues, producing genetically identical cells

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells from one parent cell, and is used for growth, tissue repair, and asexual reproduction in some organisms.

questions.questionText: Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection proposes that species change over time mainly because:

options.text: individuals with advantageous heritable variations survive and reproduce more successfully, passing those traits on
all individuals in a population are genetically identical

questions.explanation: Natural selection proposes that heritable variation exists within a population, and individuals with advantageous traits for their environment are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass those traits to offspring, gradually changing the population over time.

questions.questionText: Peppered moths in England became predominantly dark-coloured during industrial pollution because:

options.text: dark moths were better camouflaged against soot-darkened trees, avoiding predators
pollution directly changed moths' colour within their own lifetime
light-coloured moths were better camouflaged in polluted areas
moth colour has no connection to survival

questions.explanation: This is a classic example of natural selection: as pollution darkened tree bark, dark-coloured moths were better camouflaged from predators than light-coloured moths, so dark moths survived and reproduced more successfully, increasing in frequency.

questions.questionText: Selective breeding of cattle for higher milk yield is an example of:

options.text: artificial selection, where humans choose which animals breed
random mutation with no human involvement
a purely environmental change with no genetic basis

questions.explanation: Selective (artificial) breeding involves humans deliberately choosing animals with desirable traits, such as high milk yield, to breed together, increasing the frequency of that trait over generations.

questions.questionText: Which of the following would most likely provide evidence supporting evolution?

options.text: Fossil records showing gradual change in organisms over time
All species having remained completely unchanged throughout history
A complete lack of variation within any species
No similarities existing between related species

questions.explanation: Fossil records showing a gradual sequence of changes in organisms over geological time provide strong evidence supporting the theory of evolution.

questions.questionText: A population of insects exposed repeatedly to the same pesticide over many generations may develop resistance mainly because:

options.text: the pesticide causes all insects to become resistant equally
naturally resistant individuals survive pesticide exposure and reproduce, passing on resistance genes
pesticides have no effect on insect populations
insects deliberately develop resistance through learning

questions.explanation: Pesticide resistance develops through natural selection: naturally resistant individuals survive exposure and reproduce, increasing the frequency of resistance genes in the population over generations.

questions.questionText: Camouflage in an animal such as a chameleon is an example of:

options.text: an adaptation that improves survival by avoiding predators
a behaviour learned entirely from parents with no genetic basis
a feature with no survival value

questions.explanation: Camouflage is an inherited adaptation that helps an organism avoid detection by predators (or prey), increasing its chances of survival and successful reproduction.

questions.questionText: In a food web (as opposed to a simple food chain), organisms are shown to:

options.text: eat only one type of food, with no other connections
have multiple feeding relationships, showing several interconnected food chains

questions.explanation: A food web shows the multiple, interconnected feeding relationships between organisms in an ecosystem, combining several overlapping food chains, unlike a single simple food chain.

questions.questionText: A pyramid of numbers or biomass in an ecosystem typically shows:

options.text: a large number/mass of producers at the base, decreasing at each higher trophic level
an equal number/mass of organisms at every trophic level
the smallest number/mass of organisms always at the producer level

questions.explanation: Ecological pyramids generally show a large number or biomass of producers at the base, decreasing progressively at each higher trophic level, reflecting energy loss along the food chain.

questions.questionText: A primary consumer in a food chain is an organism that:

options.text: makes its own food through photosynthesis

questions.explanation: A primary consumer is a herbivore that feeds directly on producers (plants), occupying the second trophic level in a food chain.

questions.questionText: The carbon cycle is important because it:

options.text: permanently removes all carbon dioxide from the atmosphere
recycles carbon between living organisms, the atmosphere and other reservoirs through processes such as photosynthesis, respiration and decomposition
only involves plants, with no role for animals or decomposers

questions.explanation: The carbon cycle describes how carbon moves between the atmosphere, living organisms, and other reservoirs through processes such as photosynthesis (removing carbon dioxide), respiration and decomposition (releasing it), maintaining a natural balance.

questions.questionText: Overgrazing of land by livestock can lead to which environmental problem?

options.text: Improved soil fertility with no downside
Soil erosion and desertification due to loss of vegetation cover
No effect on the land at all

questions.explanation: Overgrazing removes protective vegetation cover, exposing soil to erosion by wind and water, and can lead to desertification of previously productive land.

questions.questionText: Which practice would best support sustainable use of a forest resource?

options.text: Clear-cutting the entire forest at once
Selective logging combined with replanting programmes
Preventing any regeneration of harvested trees
Ignoring the rate of tree removal entirely

questions.explanation: Selective logging (removing only some trees) combined with replanting allows continued use of forest resources while supporting long-term regeneration and sustainability.

questions.questionText: Biodiversity within an ecosystem refers to:

options.text: the total number of a single species present
the variety of different species and genetic variation within an ecosystem
only the number of predators present
the physical size of the ecosystem

questions.explanation: Biodiversity refers to the variety of species, and genetic variation within those species, present within a given ecosystem or region.

questions.questionText: A high level of pollution in a river, such as from untreated industrial or sewage waste, often results in:

options.text: increased dissolved oxygen and thriving fish populations
decreased dissolved oxygen and death of many aquatic organisms
no measurable effect on aquatic life

questions.explanation: Pollution, especially organic waste, often leads to increased microbial activity that consumes dissolved oxygen in water, reducing oxygen availability and harming or killing aquatic organisms.

questions.questionText: Quota systems limiting the number of fish that may be caught are an example of a strategy to:

options.text: conserve fish populations and support sustainable fishing
have no effect on fish stocks

questions.explanation: Fishing quotas limit how many fish can be caught, helping to prevent overfishing and support the long-term sustainability of fish populations.

questions.questionText: Competition between two species for the same limited resource (such as food or space) in an ecosystem can result in:

options.text: a reduction in the population size of one or both competing species
immediate extinction of all species involved

questions.explanation: Competition for a limited resource can reduce the population size of one or both competing species, as not all individuals are able to obtain enough of the resource to survive and reproduce successfully.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is a biotic (living) factor that can influence a population within an ecosystem?
questions.explanation: Predation is a biotic factor, involving interaction between living organisms, unlike soil pH, rainfall and temperature, which are abiotic (non-living) factors.
